name: World Café
use_case: We are organising a large event, anywhere from thirty to a few hundred people, for an evening or half a day, and we do not want the programme to be speeches and a panel. Participants should explore two or three important questions in depth in small conversation circles, change groups between rounds so that ideas travel and combine across the event, and finish with a shared picture of the themes that emerged.
strengths: turns a large audience into dozens of parallel small conversations at once
moving between tables lets ideas travel and combine across the whole room
relaxed, informal setting lowers the threshold for people who never speak at public meetings
scales from a few dozen to several hundred people with the same simple rules
the paper on each table leaves a visible trace that can be gathered into a shared picture
weaknesses: explores and connects ideas but produces no decision or ranked priorities on its own
stands or falls with the quality of the questions; vague or closed questions give small talk
the closing harvest is hard to do well with hundreds of people and is often rushed
needs a large room, many tables and at least an hour and a half to do the rounds justice
people with little time or a pressing operational issue may find the open format too loose
use_cases: A school wants its annual parents' evening to be more than the head teacher presenting slides: parents, teachers and pupils should talk together about what makes the school a good place to learn.

A municipality is consulting residents on the future of a neighbourhood and wants a public event where a hundred and fifty citizens actually exchange views with each other, not a hearing with questions from the floor.
Our annual staff conference is all keynotes and slide decks; this year leadership wants the two hundred employees to discuss the big questions facing the organisation among themselves.
A regional health network gathers patients, carers, clinicians and social workers for one afternoon to explore how care could be better joined up, before any plan is drafted.
A university department invites students, lecturers and administrators to rethink its study programme together and wants many perspectives to meet and build on one another.
